messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan came to therapy at twenty-six, referred by his primary care physician after months of declining function and a PCL-5 score of 56. He is a magazine editor, married for two years, and until recently had described his life as quietly purposeful. That sense of purpose collapsed following an encounter with police officers approximately eight months ago, during a late-night stop on his walk home from the office. What began as a request for identification escalated without warning: Rohan was pushed against a wall, his face pressed into the cold concrete, arms wrenched behind his back while officers shouted at him. He recalls the particular bite of the winter air on his exposed wrists and neck, the smell of exhaust and damp pavement, and the sensation of his body locked rigid and helpless, chest crushed flat, cheek against the ground. A female officer stood nearby, watching. He was released without charge. No one apologised. He walked the rest of the way home in silence and told his wife only that he had been stopped. He did not yet have language for what had happened to him.

In the weeks that followed, the memories did not stay in the past. When they returned, they came with the body. Rohan would find himself suddenly aware that his shoulders were drawn back and his cheek was pressed toward the floor, his muscles reproducing the exact posture of that night without his permission. Sometimes the smell of exhaust or damp concrete would arrive with the image — not as metaphor but as sensation, immediate and physical. And the memories were not neutral; they carried with them a grief so total and disorienting that he would sit at his desk unable to work, certain that something irreplaceable had been destroyed. These intrusive returns of the event fed directly into a darkening set of conclusions about himself and his future. He had come to believe, with a conviction that felt like clear-eyed realism rather than distortion, that his inability to move past what had happened proved he was a lousy coper — that other men would have recovered by now, filed it away, continued. The grief on recall only confirmed this: a stronger person, he reasoned, would not still be crying. From this belief that he was fundamentally inadequate, a broader despair followed — nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, and he was certain that nothing good could happen to him. The work he had once loved felt hollow. His marriage, though his wife remained patient, felt like something he was failing to inhabit fully.

These appraisals did not simply colour his mood; they shaped what his nervous system attended to. Convinced that he was permanently damaged and that the world held nothing restorative, Rohan found himself hypervigilant to the very cues that had been present during the assault. A drop in temperature — the particular cold of winter air against skin — could pull him back to the wall, to the concrete, to the smell. At work, the editorial office is open-plan and he frequently needs to review copy with female colleagues in small meeting rooms. Being alone with a woman had become unexpectedly charged: the female officer's silent presence during the assault had lodged in him as something threatening, and now proximity to women triggered a creeping sense of detachment, as though the room were becoming unreal and he were watching himself from a slight distance. That dissociative feeling, once it began, itself became a trigger — a signal to Rohan that he was losing his grip again, which confirmed his belief that he could not cope, which in turn sharpened his vigilance and made the next temperature shift or the next meeting with a female colleague more loaded than the last. The loop was not named but it was felt: each triggered memory deepened the appraisal of permanent damage, and each appraisal of permanent damage narrowed the world until almost everything in it could become a trigger.

What finally brought Rohan to seek help was a morning when he sat at his desk for three hours and edited nothing. His wife had noticed he was not sleeping. He came to therapy saying he did not expect to feel better — he was not sure he believed that was still possible — but that he could not continue to disappear from his own life.
